text: Chapter 11 / 19 Numerical dispersion: phase speed, group speed, and waveforms Learning goal: Use the argument of amplification to examine phase and propagation-speed error, understand waveform distortion without amplitude loss, and distinguish physical dispersion. A waveform changes if its crests travel at the wrong speeds, even when amplitude is nearly preserved. Numerical dispersion is a wavenumber-dependent departure of phase evolution from the exact equation. Measure it separately from numerical dissipation. Phase speed describes motion of a wave crest, while group speed describes an envelope occupying a narrow wavenumber band. One group speed does not describe every arbitrary broadband waveform. Read the argument of a complex multiplier With time dependence exp(-iωt), write G=|G|exp(iφ) and read the real numerical angular frequency as-φ/Δt. Choose a continuous phase branch; do not turn a jump from π to-π into a physical speed discontinuity. Constant-speed advection has a constant reference speed For exact constant-speed advection, both phase and group speed equal a. Using the discrete G expresses speed ratios in terms of θ. The figure uses 0<θ<π, avoiding the sign and branch ambiguity at the Nyquist endpoint. Distinguish physical dispersion If a medium or equation itself has wavenumber-dependent propagation speed, dispersion is physical. Our reference is nondispersive constant-speed advection, so deviations of the plotted ratios are numerical. Always show their dependence on steps and grid resolution. A small worked example Compute the argument of complex G to obtain the phase-speed ratio. Evaluate group speed from the derivative of G, and test it against a separate small-difference derivative of the phase. The advection runs in this edition transport a sum of two sine waves. Group speeds in the figure are evaluated from the discrete symbol; they are not direct measurements tracking the center of a localized wave packet. from cmath import phase from lab import symbol nu, theta = 0.6, 0.4 G = symbol("lax-wendroff", theta, nu) phase_speed_ratio = -phase(G)/(nu*theta) print(phase_speed_ratio) At high wavenumbers, amplitude damping and phase error can both become large. Phase measurements of extremely weak components can also become unreliable, so read them together with |G|. Figure 11: Phase- and group-speed ratios obtained from G. The exact value is 1. Do not confuse short grid-wavelength behavior with the physical speeds of the continuous equation. Show answer No: an incorrect phase is still an error. Amplitude preservation and propagation-speed accuracy are separate. Question 2: What can go wrong when directly differencing arg G? Show answer A branch jump from π to-π can produce an artificially huge derivative. Check continuity of the phase branch. Common pitfalls Do not assign the group-speed formula uniformly to an arbitrary broadband waveform. Do not try to remove physical dispersion as if it were numerical error. Key points Measure phase and amplitude separately. Relate speed at each wavenumber to its resolution.
